title: Redwood Shadow Evals / Shadow Traffic - technical deep dive (safe model upgrades)
summary: Apex FinServ evaluated Redwood’s upcoming “Shadow Evals” capability for upgrading models safely using production-shaped traffic. Redwood walked through request mirroring (sampling + allowlists), async shadow execution that does not block or change primary responses, linking primary and shadow via request_id, and operational guardrails (kill switch, budgets, rate limits, backpressure, drop accounting). Applied ML described judge scoring and which metrics are safe for gating. Security covered retention/redaction options, residency controls, and access/audit expectations. Apex asked about latency blast radius, capacity planning, UI/Console visibility, and how results can halt a rollout automatically.
topics: Shadow traffic architecture (mirroring point, async runner, request_id linking). Shadow targets (model/version/quant profile/prompt config) and policy controls (sampling %, allowlist, region, route). Metrics: similarity/format adherence, safety outcomes, LLM-as-judge win-rate, rubric scoring, latency/cost deltas. Console dashboards and rollout policy gates. Guardrails: kill switch, capacity budgets, queue backpressure, cardinality limits. Security/compliance: redaction, retention, residency, restricted access and audit logs.
questions: Can shadow ever impact primary p99 latency? What happens if shadow queue backs up—do you drop or slow? Can we constrain shadowing to specific customers/tenants and regions? Can we shadow a new quantization profile (int8/int4) vs baseline? How do you handle PII in prompts/outputs used for judge scoring? What retention options exist and can we keep shadow payloads out of logging entirely? Can rollout automation stop a canary if judge win-rate drops below threshold? How are metrics aggregated to avoid high cardinality (prompt hash / request_id, etc.)?

Apex to provide 2–3 candidate routes for the pilot (one chat, one structured output / JSON route) plus baseline success metrics.
Redwood to confirm residency + retention defaults and send security posture notes (redaction options, access controls, audit logging).
Schedule follow-up: Console walkthrough of Shadow Evals dashboard and example rollout gate configuration.

Logan Wright: Provide a sample of the shadow_eval metric dimensions + cardinality guardrails and what tags are allowed (by 2025-11-12).
Jonas Weber: Share judge rubric template recommendations for “upgrade safety” comparisons and what to gate on vs observe-only (by 2025-11-12).

transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Redwood Shadow Evals / Shadow Traffic - technical deep dive (safe model upgrades)
Date: 2025-11-05
Time: 4:00pm - 4:56pm PT
Duration: 56 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Marissa Cole, Dylan Brooks, Jada Williams, Logan Wright, Jonas Weber, Naomi Feldman, Sean Gallagher
Apex FinServ: Rachel Kim, Nate Alvarez, Priya Desai, Tom Becker, Evan Liu

(Recording started)

[00:00] Marissa Cole: Cool. Thanks everyone for making time. I know you all are looking at a model upgrade, and the theme is “how do we do it without surprises.” Today we’ll go deeper on Shadow Evals—how we mirror traffic, run candidates, and collect metrics without touching the end user response.

[00:21] Rachel Kim: Yep. Our main concern is we don’t want to do a big bang model swap. We want like, production-shaped data, but… no user impact.

[00:31] Marissa Cole: Exactly. That’s the principle. It’s shadow execution—async. Primary response is still the primary model. Shadow results go to telemetry.

[00:40] Dylan Brooks: And we’ll be honest about what’s “beta” here. But the core invariants are strict: the primary path cannot block on shadow. Shadow can fail, get dropped, be rate limited—primary should not care.

[00:55] Tom Becker: So where does mirroring happen? Gateway? Runtime? We’ve been burned by “oh it’s just a mirror” and then suddenly you add work in the request handler.

[01:07] Jada Williams: Good question. We’re implementing the mirroring hook at the data plane boundary, but it’s decoupled. Think: request comes in, primary executes as usual. In parallel we enqueue a minimal shadow job—metadata + redacted payload depending on policy—and the shadow runner pulls from that queue.

[01:28] Nate Alvarez: So you’re not doing like, a synchronous fan-out call to two models inside the same request?

[01:34] Jada Williams: Correct, not synchronous fan-out. The “shadow runner” is a worker service. There is a strict timeout and budget on enqueue. If enqueue can’t happen fast, we just don’t shadow that request.

[01:50] Sean Gallagher: From SRE side, the requirement is basically: primary p99 should be unchanged within the noise. We have a perf canary specifically to watch for regressions when shadow is enabled.

[02:02] Tom Becker: Okay. But enqueue itself is still in the primary request thread, no?

[02:06] Jada Williams: It is, but it’s bounded and non-blocking. The pattern is “best effort” with very small CPU work. If queue is unavailable or saturated, we drop shadow and increment a drop counter. No retries on the primary thread.

[02:22] Logan Wright: And we record why it was dropped—budget exceeded, queue depth, rate limit, etc.—so you don’t get fooled by “everything looks good” when actually you weren’t shadowing anything.

[02:34] Rachel Kim: That drop accounting matters. We’ve seen systems that quietly stop collecting data.

[02:39] Marissa Cole: Yeah. The Console will show a “shadow coverage” metric. Like sampled vs executed vs dropped.

[02:48] Evan Liu: Can I just check: “Shadow Evals” is the same thing as “shadow traffic,” right? Not like… separate product?

[02:54] Marissa Cole: Internally we say “Shadow Traffic” for the data plane behavior and “Shadow Evals” for the Console view + scoring + rollout gates. But it’s one feature set.

[03:05] Nate Alvarez: How do you select the shadow target? We want to compare, for example, model version, maybe quantization profile, maybe prompt config changes.

[03:14] Jada Williams: It’s expressed in route policy. Per route you can define one or more shadow targets. A “target” can be a model identifier plus config like version pin, quant profile, and prompt template reference.

[03:28] Dylan Brooks: And then you can configure sampling percent, allowlist by customer, region constraints, and budgets. Like “only do 1% shadow in us-east, only for these tenants.”

[03:41] Priya Desai: Tenant allowlisting is required for us. We cannot sample across everyone for a beta.

[03:46] Marissa Cole: That’s supported. It’s one of the top enterprise requirements.

[03:51] Priya Desai: Also data residency. We operate EU + US and we can’t have prompts leaving region.

[03:59] Naomi Feldman: On residency: Shadow execution follows the same region routing constraints as the primary, and we can enforce “shadow targets must be in-region.” For storage, we can configure retention per region and ensure data stays in that boundary.

[04:16] Priya Desai: And what about prompts being stored at all? For judging you might store the prompt + completion.

[04:23] Naomi Feldman: We have redaction controls and “store nothing” modes. The default for shadow telemetry is metrics-first—store derived scores and minimal metadata. If you enable payload sampling for debugging or judge audits, that’s gated behind restricted access controls and short retention.

[04:43] Rachel Kim: Can we do judge scoring without storing raw text?

[04:46] Jonas Weber: Yes. The judge itself needs text in memory to score, but we don’t have to persist it. We can emit only the score, e.g., win/loss/tie plus confidence, and some structured tags like “format_valid=true.”

[05:02] Nate Alvarez: Wait, what is the judge? Another model call?

[05:06] Jonas Weber: It can be. We call it “LLM-as-judge.” It’s a rubric prompt that compares baseline output and candidate output for the same request. It returns a preference plus rubric sub-scores.

[05:20] Nate Alvarez: That’s expensive.

[05:22] Jonas Weber: It can be, yes. That’s why it’s optional and policy-driven. Some teams start with cheap signals: output length, JSON parse validity, safety policy outcomes, similarity metrics. Then they run judge on a smaller sample or on “high value” routes.

[05:41] Logan Wright: And we track cost deltas too. Like tokens in/out and approximate dollars, per target.

[05:48] Tom Becker: When you say tokens… is that for both baseline and shadow, or just shadow?

[05:53] Logan Wright: Both. Primary already has token accounting. Shadow runner reports its own. We can show “candidate is +12% output tokens” or “latency +80ms p95” etc.

[06:06] Rachel Kim: Can you show us a typical metric set you expect to gate on?

[06:10] Jonas Weber: For gating, we recommend very conservative metrics. For example: structured output routes—“format adherence” (valid JSON, schema match), safety classification delta, and judge win-rate where judge is calibrated.

[06:26] Jonas Weber: What we don’t recommend gating on: raw embedding cosine similarity of outputs for open-ended tasks. It’s noisy. Use that as an exploratory metric.

[06:37] Evan Liu: Our “assistant” route is partly open-ended. But we have some strict sections like “must include citations.”

[06:44] Jonas Weber: That’s a good fit for rubric-based judging. Like “has citations,” “doesn’t hallucinate citations,” “answers the question.”

[06:54] Dylan Brooks: And you can set the rollout policy: “halt canary if win-rate drops more than X% vs baseline” or “if format_valid falls below 99.5%.”

[07:06] Tom Becker: “Halt canary” means your system can actually stop the rollout automatically?

[07:10] Dylan Brooks: Yes, via the rollouts policy engine. Shadow metrics become a signal the rollout can reference.

[07:19] Rachel Kim: Is that GA or beta?

[07:22] Marissa Cole: The gating integration is in the beta plan, but we’ll probably start with “alert only” for early pilots. Some customers want a human-in-the-loop phase.

[07:34] Nate Alvarez: How is the primary request linked to shadow execution? For our analysis we’d want to join on request id.

[07:41] Jada Williams: We propagate a request_id through both. The shadow job includes the primary request_id and a shadow_run_id. In telemetry we can join primary metadata (route, region, customer tier, etc.) with shadow outputs and scores.

[07:59] Logan Wright: And we can also attach tags like “shadow_target=llama-3.1-70b-q4” or whatever. With cardinality constraints.

[08:10] Tom Becker: Yeah, cardinality. Please don’t explode our metrics.

[08:13] Logan Wright: Totally. We have strict tag allowlists. No raw request ids in metrics tags. request_id exists in trace logs for debugging, but metrics are aggregated. Also we bucket stuff like prompt version rather than raw prompt hash, unless you explicitly opt into a safe, low-cardinality label.

[08:31] Priya Desai: You said “trace logs.” Are shadow traces separate from primary traces?

[08:36] Logan Wright: They’re separate spans but same trace id linkage is possible. It depends on integration, but the idea is: the primary trace includes a small “shadow_enqueued” span; the shadow runner has its own trace referencing the same request_id. In the Console you can pivot between them.

[08:54] Tom Becker: I’m going to push on this: if shadow runner is overloaded, can it cause primary to slow, like by saturating GPU pools? Even if you decouple with a queue, the GPU is shared.

[09:07] Sean Gallagher: Great. That’s why we have capacity budgets. Shadow runs are scheduled on a separate pool or separated capacity slice, depending on deployment. In hosted/dedicated, we can reserve a portion for shadow or cap it with rate limiting. In private deployments, we recommend separate node pool or at least strict quotas.

[09:28] Tom Becker: So you can guarantee it doesn’t steal capacity from production?

[09:31] Sean Gallagher: “Guarantee” depends on whether you want separate hardware. But we can enforce budgets so it won’t exceed, say, 2% GPU time. If it hits the cap, it drops. The main protection is: shadow is always lower priority.

[09:46] Nate Alvarez: Is that like K8s priority classes? Or internal scheduler?

[09:49] Sean Gallagher: Similar concept. In hosted we control the scheduler. In private we integrate with your scheduler. But in all cases: shadow work is preemptible.

[10:01] Dylan Brooks: There’s also a global kill switch. So if you see anything weird—utilization spike, queue growth—you can disable all shadowing immediately, no deploy.

[10:12] Tom Becker: Where is that kill switch? Console? API?

[10:15] Dylan Brooks: Both. There’s an admin control in Console and an API endpoint. Also per-route disable.

[10:22] Rachel Kim: If you kill switch, what happens to in-flight shadow jobs?

[10:26] Jada Williams: We stop scheduling new ones. In-flight ones either finish or are cancelled depending on worker configuration. But again it’s not user impacting.

[10:35] Evan Liu: Quick product question: do we pay for the extra tokens used in shadow?

[10:40] Marissa Cole: For beta we’re still finalizing packaging. The intent is you can attribute shadow cost separately and set quotas. We’ll propose a “shadow sampling quota” by account.

[10:53] Rachel Kim: Okay, we can talk commercial later. For now we need the safety story.

[11:00] Priya Desai: And the data story.

[11:02] Marissa Cole: Yep.

[11:04] Naomi Feldman: On data classification: We treat shadow payloads as the same classification as production payloads. The default is minimal retention. We can configure: store only metrics; store redacted snippets; store full payload for a short window with approvals.

[11:22] Priya Desai: “Approvals” as in…

[11:24] Naomi Feldman: RBAC, audit logs, and a restricted group. If someone wants access to raw shadow samples, it’s logged. We can integrate with your SSO/SAML and require MFA. Also, the “raw sample store” can be disabled entirely.

[11:44] Nate Alvarez: For judge scoring, what’s the failure mode? Like if judge model drifts, or judge is inconsistent.

[11:51] Jonas Weber: Great callout. LLM judges are not ground truth. We do calibration, and we recommend using a stable judge model + prompt version pinned. Also treat judge as comparative signal. In early phase, we want to correlate judge with offline evals and some human review.

[12:12] Rachel Kim: So we shouldn’t auto-rollback solely on judge win rate day one.

[12:16] Jonas Weber: Correct. Our guidance: start “observe only,” then “alert,” then “gate.” And gate on metrics with low ambiguity (format correctness, safety).

[12:28] Dylan Brooks: The rollout policy can say “if judge win-rate drops >3% AND format_valid drop >0.2% then hold.” You can combine signals.

[12:40] Logan Wright: We also compute confidence intervals because sample sizes can be small. You don’t want to stop a rollout on five requests.

[12:50] Tom Becker: THANK YOU. Please.

[12:52] (crosstalk)

[12:54] Logan Wright: Yeah, so the dashboard shows n, coverage, and we can set minimum sample thresholds before gates apply.

[13:04] Nate Alvarez: Is it possible to target only a subset of prompt patterns? Like only the “account summary” use case within a route.

[13:10] Dylan Brooks: Within a route, today the policy is route-level plus tenant/region. We could add conditional matching on request attributes, but that’s not in MVP.

[13:21] Rachel Kim: We can split routes if needed.

[13:23] Dylan Brooks: Exactly.

[13:25] Tom Becker: Another SRE concern: if shadow runner is broken, do we page? Or is it non-critical.

[13:31] Sean Gallagher: It’s non-critical to production availability, but it can page based on your preferences. We have alerting on queue depth, shadow error rate, and drop count anomalies. But we keep it separate from primary SLO alerts.

[13:50] Tom Becker: Good. We don’t want to be woken up because your judge model is unhappy.

[13:55] Jonas Weber: (laughs) Yeah. Shadow-only failures should not page primary on-call.

[14:01] Logan Wright: In dashboards we label “shadow health” vs “primary health” clearly.

[14:07] Evan Liu: Can we see a sample dashboard? Like what’s on the page.

[14:11] Marissa Cole: I can describe it. There’s a Shadow Evals view per route. Time series: judge win-rate, format adherence, safety pass rates, latency deltas. Then breakdown by target. Filters: time window, region, tenant allowlist. And a coverage panel.

[14:33] Rachel Kim: Is that in Redwood Console or Grafana?

[14:36] Marissa Cole: Both exist. Console is the customer-facing one; Grafana is our internal plus some customers with advanced setups. But we’ll focus on Console for you.

[14:47] Nate Alvarez: On the architecture again: what exactly is stored in the shadow job? Is it the full request body? We have some very large contexts.

[14:55] Jada Williams: It can be. But we can configure truncation and redaction. Also, to avoid big payload movement, we can store a reference pointer if the payload already exists in a safe store, though that’s more complex.

[15:11] Nate Alvarez: Sorry, does that mean you’re copying the full context across the network twice?

[15:17] Jada Williams: Potentially, yes, if you configure it that way. Most customers start with smaller sampling and maybe only on routes with manageable context. We also support not shadowing requests above a size threshold.

[15:32] Tom Becker: That’s important. Payload size itself can be an SLO risk.

[15:35] Jada Williams: Agreed. We’ll have policy validation like “max_shadow_payload_bytes.”

[15:41] Rachel Kim: For our pilot, we’d choose smaller routes first.

[15:44] Evan Liu: We can do “account FAQ” route first.

[15:48] Nate Alvarez: And maybe the structured JSON extraction route. That’s the one that tends to break.

[15:53] Jonas Weber: Structured route is perfect for shadow. Easy to score.

[16:00] Priya Desai: For SOC2 and audit, can we get audit logs showing who enabled shadowing and when, and who accessed any raw samples?

[16:09] Naomi Feldman: Yes. Control changes (enable/disable, sampling percent, target changes) are logged. Access to restricted shadow payload samples is logged. We can export audit logs or integrate with your SIEM.

[16:26] Priya Desai: Okay.

[16:28] Tom Becker: What about incident response. If we see a capacity spike, is the guidance just “kill switch”?

[16:34] Sean Gallagher: First step yes: kill switch or set sampling to 0. Then check queue depth, worker error rates, GPU utilization. We have a runbook with verification queries and “confirm no shadow requests are executing.”

[16:52] Tom Becker: Great. We’d want that runbook shared if we pilot.

[16:55] Marissa Cole: We can share a customer-facing version.

[17:00] Nate Alvarez: How long does it take for the system to reflect config changes? If we change sampling 1% to 0%.

[17:06] Jada Williams: It’s control-plane propagated quickly—on the order of seconds. No deploy.

[17:13] Rachel Kim: I want to check on the “model upgrade” path. The target we’re thinking is moving from one vendor model to an open model, maybe Llama variant, or at least a new version. We want to do apples-to-apples.

[17:28] Jonas Weber: That’s exactly the intention. Shadow target can be a different model family. We compare baseline output to candidate output. For tasks where output format differs, we can normalize before judging.

[17:42] Nate Alvarez: Normalize how? Like stripping whitespace, JSON reordering.

[17:46] Jonas Weber: Yes. Canonicalization for JSON, ignore ordering if your schema allows it, and compare structured fields. Also we can parse citations section separately.

[17:59] Evan Liu: How do you handle tool calling / function calling? We’re using function calls for some routes.

[18:05] Dylan Brooks: Shadow supports tool calling too. But we have to be careful: in shadow mode, tool calls should not execute side effects. So we either stub tools or run “dry-run” tool execution.

[18:20] Rachel Kim: We absolutely cannot have side effects.

[18:23] Dylan Brooks: Yep. That’s non-negotiable. In shadow, tools are disabled by default or run in a sandbox. The system records what tool call would have been made, but does not perform it.

[18:39] Tom Becker: Great.

[18:41] Nate Alvarez: For the shadow runner, is it running on the same inference cluster? If it’s separate, does that skew performance metrics.

[18:49] Sean Gallagher: There’s a tradeoff. If it’s separate hardware, your latency numbers won’t match exactly. If it’s shared, you risk contention. Our usual recommendation is: run on similar hardware but with a budgeted slice. Then you can interpret deltas with caution. For absolute latency, you can run controlled load tests.

[19:13] Logan Wright: In the dashboard we emphasize “relative deltas” and show confidence bands. We can also tag “hardware_class” so you know if comparisons are fair.

[19:24] Rachel Kim: Okay.

[19:26] Priya Desai: Another privacy question. If you’re doing redaction, what is redacted? Names, account numbers, emails, etc.

[19:33] Naomi Feldman: We support configurable PII filters: emails, phone numbers, SSNs, account numbers patterns. Also allowlist-based: only store certain fields. But be careful—LLM text is messy. We recommend “metrics-only” retention for regulated content unless you really need samples.

[19:57] Nate Alvarez: If we do metrics-only, how do we debug regressions?

[20:01] Jonas Weber: Typically you’ll enable a very small, approved sample capture, like 0.01%, redacted, short retention, restricted access, just to look at examples when a metric trips.

[20:14] Tom Becker: And that’s separate from the general shadow sampling.

[20:17] Jonas Weber: Exactly.

[20:19] Dylan Brooks: Also, we can integrate with your own storage if you prefer. But again, that’s beyond MVP.

[20:30] Evan Liu: Can we use this to compare prompt changes, not just model upgrades.

[20:35] Marissa Cole: Yes. That’s actually a common use case—prompt template v2 as shadow target.

[20:41] Nate Alvarez: What about KV cache? Sorry, “K V cash” (laughs). If shadow runs same prompt, do you benefit from caching? That could hide cost.

[20:51] Jada Williams: Shadow execution is isolated. We don’t want it to interfere with primary caching or batching. So caches are separate. That means it’s not “free.”

[21:03] Sean Gallagher: And again, it’s preemptible. If primary needs the GPU, shadow yields.

[21:10] Tom Becker: That’s good.

[21:12] Logan Wright: From telemetry side, we tag whether a shadow run used cache hits in its own context, but it won’t share caches with primary.

[21:23] Rachel Kim: Another question: how do you prevent shadow from accidentally changing the user response? I know you said it doesn’t, but like… code paths.

[21:32] Dylan Brooks: The primary response is computed and streamed back to client. Shadow runs after that, or at least in parallel but not in the same response pipeline. We don’t merge. There’s no code path that swaps responses.

[21:46] Jada Williams: We also have tests and invariants like “shadow must never block streaming.” If shadow fails, primary is unaffected.

[21:56] Tom Becker: Okay.

[21:58] Marissa Cole: Maybe we should walk through a request example quickly.

[22:02] Marissa Cole: User calls /chat/completions on Route A. The request hits our gateway. We route to primary target (say model X). Response streams back as usual. In parallel, if policy says sample=1% and tenant allowlisted and within region, we enqueue job: request_id, route_id, primary target id, plus payload (maybe redacted) and shadow target config. Worker picks it up, runs candidate model, computes metrics (format checks, judge if enabled), emits shadow_eval events. Console aggregates and shows deltas.

[22:41] Rachel Kim: That helps.

[22:43] Nate Alvarez: The join between primary and shadow—does it happen in your telemetry pipeline or do we have to do it.

[22:50] Logan Wright: We do it in our pipeline. You query by route/time window and we return aggregated metrics. You can also export raw event-level data if your plan includes it, but again, cardinality and privacy controls apply.

[23:10] Tom Becker: What’s your event volume? If we have 10k RPS on one route and sample 1%, that’s 100 RPS shadow. That’s still big.

[23:20] Sean Gallagher: That’s why budgets exist. You might do 0.1% to start, or cap shadow RPS. You can set both sampling percentage and absolute rate caps.

[23:33] Tom Becker: Good.

[23:35] Marissa Cole: We’ll propose safe defaults in beta: sampling off by default, caps low.

[23:42] Priya Desai: And default retention minimal.

[23:45] Naomi Feldman: Yep.

[23:47] Evan Liu: How long until we can try it? We have a Q1 upgrade planned.

[23:53] Marissa Cole: Beta is staged, but we’re targeting select enterprise accounts in November/December. If we agree on pilot routes and data constraints, you’re a strong candidate.

[24:07] Rachel Kim: Okay.

[24:09] Nate Alvarez: For the judge scoring, do we bring our own judge model? Or do you provide.

[24:15] Jonas Weber: We can provide a default judge configuration. Some customers bring their own for data residency or policy reasons. The judge prompt + model version can be pinned.

[24:29] Priya Desai: If judge is a third-party model, that’s a compliance problem.

[24:34] Jonas Weber: Understood. We can run judge on an in-region Redwood-hosted model, or in your private deployment. It can be the same platform.

[24:46] Tom Becker: But then you’re doubling inference load. Candidate model + judge model.

[24:51] Jonas Weber: Right. That’s why it’s optional and can be sampled at a lower rate than shadow itself. Example: shadow candidate at 1%, judge at 0.1%.

[25:06] Logan Wright: And the pipeline supports “judge coverage” metric so you know how many were scored.

[25:12] Rachel Kim: Nice.

[25:14] Dylan Brooks: Also, you can configure judge only on failures, like if format_invalid triggers, then run judge. That’s not in MVP but it’s in the direction.

[25:27] Nate Alvarez: Got it.

[25:30] Tom Becker: What about timeouts. Shadow can run long if candidate model is slower.

[25:35] Jada Williams: Shadow runner has max execution time. If it exceeds, we mark it timed out and emit that as a metric. No retries by default.

[25:47] Sean Gallagher: We also watch “shadow timeouts rate.” It’s useful to identify candidates that are too slow.

[25:56] Evan Liu: And the user never sees that timeout.

[25:58] Jada Williams: Correct.

[26:01] Priya Desai: I want to confirm access controls. Who at Redwood can see our shadow data.

[26:06] Naomi Feldman: By default, only your tenant’s admins and limited Redwood support roles if you grant. For raw payload samples, it’s more restricted and requires explicit enablement and auditable approvals. We can also do “no Redwood access” mode for private deployments.

[26:29] Rachel Kim: That’s good.

[26:31] Nate Alvarez: One more technical: can we shadow across different system prompts? Like baseline uses system prompt v1, candidate uses v2.

[26:39] Dylan Brooks: Yes. The target config can reference a prompt config. For fairness, you can pin both and compare.

[26:47] Jonas Weber: Just make sure your eval rubric is aligned. Otherwise judge might prefer “more verbose” rather than “more correct.”

[26:58] Nate Alvarez: Yeah.

[27:00] Marissa Cole: Okay, we’re at the halfway point. Anything we didn’t cover that’s critical.

[27:06] Tom Becker: I want to know: if we do this in dedicated capacity, can you segregate shadow GPU pool from prod GPU pool.

[27:13] Sean Gallagher: Yes. In Dedicated we can allocate a separate pool for shadow runner, or assign a smaller slice with strict caps. It’s configuration.

[27:25] Tom Becker: Okay.

[27:26] Rachel Kim: For pilot, we’d prefer dedicated because we need predictability.

[27:30] Marissa Cole: Understood.

[27:32] Evan Liu: What about A/B tests. We already do some A/B on prompts.

[27:36] Dylan Brooks: Shadow complements A/B. A/B changes user experience; shadow doesn’t. You can use shadow to get confidence, then run a small A/B canary with real user impact.

[27:50] Rachel Kim: That’s the workflow we want.

[27:53] Priya Desai: I also want documentation for your redaction patterns and retention defaults.

[27:58] Naomi Feldman: We’ll send a summary after the call.

[28:02] Marissa Cole: Great. Let’s do a quick recap and next steps.

[28:06] Marissa Cole: Recap: shadow is async and never blocks primary response; policy controls sampling + allowlists + region; budgets and kill switch; metrics include format/safety/judge plus latency and cost deltas; retention/redaction are configurable with metrics-only default.

[28:29] Marissa Cole: Next: we’ll send beta one-pager and policy schema; you’ll send us 2–3 candidate routes and your data classification constraints; then we schedule a Console dashboard walkthrough.

[28:43] Rachel Kim: Sounds good.

[28:45] Tom Becker: Yep.

[28:46] Priya Desai: Works.

[28:48] Nate Alvarez: Thanks.

[28:50] Marissa Cole: Thanks everyone.

(Recording ended)
